clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic variants in the OCA2 gene (formerly the P gene) and is the commonest form of oculocutaneous albinism in sub-Saharan African populations.
Unlike tyrosinase-negative OCA1A, some melanin is usually present, so hair may be pale yellow to light brown and can darken through childhood, and pigmented naevi and freckles may develop.
Ocular features are constant: congenital nystagmus, foveal hypoplasia, iris transillumination, reduced visual acuity, photophobia and misrouting of optic fibres at the chiasm.
The OCA2 locus lies within the 15q11-q13 region, so albinism can accompany Prader-Willi or Angelman syndrome when a deletion unmasks a variant on the other allele.
'Brown OCA' is an allelic variant of OCA2 with light-brown hair and skin and grey-to-hazel irides.
Skin is highly ultraviolet-sensitive, so lifelong photoprotection and dermatological surveillance for cutaneous malignancy are essential.
Visual acuity is reduced but typically stable and non-progressive; refractive correction and low-vision aids are helpful.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive; molecular confirmation and genetic counselling guide recurrence-risk advice.
reference.pathophysiology: OCA2 results from loss-of-function variants in the OCA2 gene on chromosome 15q, which encodes the P protein, a melanosomal transmembrane polypeptide. The P protein is thought to regulate melanosomal pH and the processing, stability and trafficking of tyrosinase, and thereby the maturation of melanosomes and eumelanin synthesis. Reduced P-protein function lowers melanin production in skin, hair and the eye, although some residual tyrosinase activity usually persists, accounting for the partial and often age-progressive pigmentation that distinguishes OCA2 from tyrosinase-negative OCA1A. Deficient ocular melanin during development disrupts foveal maturation and the normal decussation of retinal ganglion-cell axons at the optic chiasm, producing foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus and chiasmal misrouting.
additionalDifferentials: Oculocutaneous albinism type 1 (TYR) — usually more severe, with little or no pigment at birth.
Oculocutaneous albinism type 3 (TYRP1) — reddish rufous phenotype.
Oculocutaneous albinism type 4 (SLC45A2) — often clinically indistinguishable, requiring molecular testing.
Other OCA subtypes such as OCA6 (SLC24A5) and OCA7.
Ocular albinism (GPR143, X-linked) — ocular features with near-normal skin.
Syndromic albinism — Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome and Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
Prader-Willi or Angelman syndrome with associated hypopigmentation.
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive ophthalmological assessment — visual acuity, nystagmus, iris transillumination and refraction.
Optical coherence tomography to document foveal hypoplasia.
Visual evoked potentials to detect chiasmal misrouting.
Molecular genetic testing — an oculocutaneous albinism gene panel or sequencing including the OCA2 gene.
Dermatological examination and cutaneous malignancy surveillance.
Assessment for syndromic features (bleeding and infection history) to exclude Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes.
redFlags: New, changing or ulcerating skin lesions suggesting basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma or melanoma.
Easy bruising, epistaxis or a bleeding tendency pointing to Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome.
Recurrent severe infections or a silvery hair sheen suggesting Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
Developmental delay, hypotonia or dysmorphism raising the possibility of a 15q deletion syndrome.
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is normal and visual impairment, although lifelong, is usually stable and non-progressive. The principal preventable morbidity is ultraviolet-induced skin cancer, which rigorous photoprotection and regular skin surveillance substantially reduce.
pitfalls: Assuming all albinism is tyrosinase-negative OCA1 and missing the milder, pigment-permitting OCA2.
Overlooking syndromic causes such as Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes that carry systemic risks.
Failing to arrange visual evoked potentials, so chiasmal misrouting is missed.
Interpreting age-related darkening of hair as evidence against the diagnosis.
Relying on phenotype alone to separate OCA2 from OCA4, which requires molecular testing.
management: No curative treatment; lifelong rigorous photoprotection with high-factor broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing and sun avoidance
Regular dermatological surveillance with dermoscopy for cutaneous malignancy and prompt excision of suspicious lesions
Optimisation of vision with refractive correction, tinted or photochromic lenses for photophobia and low-vision aids and rehabilitation
Orthoptic management of congenital nystagmus and strabismus, with surgery in selected cases
Assessment for Prader-Willi or Angelman syndrome where a 15q11-q13 deletion is suspected
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive OCA2 inheritance with testing of at-risk relatives
Multidisciplinary care with educational and occupational low-vision support
